title: How can four different fractional units add up to one?
description: One circle must be filled with four different fractional units. We start from a sum that is already known, split one piece into two smaller different pieces, and check each split by adding in a common unit.
teaching_notes: One idea: build a new sum from a known one by splitting one unit into two different smaller units, and check the split in one common unit. Watch for students who split a unit into two equal pieces, which repeats a unit.

video_script.why: The child builds new sums from a known one by splitting a unit into two different smaller units, and checks each split by adding in a common unit.
video_script.substitution: The book's circle, with one piece cut into two smaller pieces of different units, so the circle stays exactly full.
video_script.anchor: one circle to be filled with four pieces, each a different fractional unit, as in the book
video_script.payoff_line: Four different fractional units can make one in six different ways
video_script.fraction_reading: one half, one third, one fourth, one fifth, one sixth, one seventh, one eighth, one ninth, one tenth, one twelfth, one fifteenth, one eighteenth, one twentieth, one twenty fourth, one forty second, six twelfths, three twelfths, two twelfths, twelve twelfths
never_show: the list of all six sums before the answer beat
maths_rules: start from 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1 and split 1/6 into two different fractional units
ground demo: 1/2 = 3/6 = 2/6 + 1/6 = 1/3 + 1/6 on a circle cut into 6 equal parts
video_script.design: One idea: split one unit of a known sum into two different smaller units, and check by adding in one common unit. The circle stays on the board from start to end.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a puzzle from your book, and it goes one step further.
<bookmark mark='circle'/>This time a circle must be filled with four pieces.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>All four must be different fractional units. Can you find one way to do it?

beats.on_screen: the circle holds still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a smaller circle cut into 6 equal parts; 3 parts shaded as 1/2; the 3 parts split into 2 parts labelled 1/3 and 1 part labelled 1/6; the circle stays full

marks.demo: a smaller circle cut into 6 equal parts appears
marks.split: the 3 parts separate into 2 parts labelled 1/3 and 1 part labelled 1/6
marks.full: the circle glows to show it is still exactly full

narration: <bookmark mark='demo'/>First look at how one piece can be split into two smaller pieces.
<bookmark mark='half'/>Take a circle cut into six equal parts. One half is three of those parts.
<bookmark mark='split'/>Split those three parts into two parts and one part. The two parts are one third, and the one part is one sixth.
<bookmark mark='full'/>The circle is still exactly full.

beats.on_screen: Given: one whole circle, and four pieces that are all different fractional units

marks.given: the whole circle and the rule all different are written on the working board

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, one whole circle, and four pieces that are all different fractional units.

beats.on_screen: To find: ways to fill the circle with four different fractional units

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find ways to fill the circle with four different fractional units.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: start from 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1; split 1/6 into two different smaller fractional units

marks.start: 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1 is written and the circle is full with 3 pieces
marks.split: the 1/6 piece glows and a split line appears across it

narration: <bookmark mark='start'/>Step one, start from the sum in your book. One half, one third and one sixth make one.
<bookmark mark='split'/>We need four pieces, so split one sixth into two smaller pieces of different units.

marks.seven: the circle is cut into 42 equal parts
marks.parts: 1/7 shows as 6 parts and 1/42 shows as 1 part
marks.sixth: 6/42 + 1/42 = 7/42 = 1/6 is written and the 7 parts match the 1/6 piece
marks.more: 1/8 + 1/24, 1/9 + 1/18 and 1/10 + 1/15 appear, each with a tick for 1/6

narration: <bookmark mark='seven'/>Step two, we change to a common bottom number the same way as the example in your book. Cut the circle into forty two equal parts.
<bookmark mark='parts'/>One seventh is six parts, and one forty second is one part.
<bookmark mark='sixth'/>Seven parts out of forty two make one sixth, so the split is right.
<bookmark mark='more'/>One sixth is also one eighth and one twenty fourth. It is also one ninth and one eighteenth. The last is one tenth and one fifteenth.

marks.half: 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 1 is written and the two 1/4 pieces glow
marks.fourth: one 1/4 piece glows and a split line appears across it

narration: <bookmark mark='half'/>Step three, there is another start. One half, one fourth and one fourth make one.
<bookmark mark='fourth'/>The two fourths are the same, so split one fourth into two different units.
<bookmark mark='twenty'/>One fourth is one fifth and one twentieth, because four twentieths and one twentieth make five twentieths.
<bookmark mark='twelve'/>One fourth is also one sixth and one twelfth, because two twelfths and one twelfth make three twelfths.

marks.back: the four pieces slide into the circle cut into 12 equal parts
marks.add: 6/12 + 3/12 + 2/12 + 1/12 = 12/12 = 1 is written and the circle is full

narration: <bookmark mark='back'/>Step four, check one of them by putting it back in the question. Use twelfths.
<bookmark mark='add'/>Six twelfths, three twelfths, two twelfths and one twelfth add up to twelve twelfths, which is one whole.

marks.ans: the six sums appear in a column, each ending with = 1

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Four different fractional units can make one in six different ways.
<bookmark mark='first'/>One half, one third, one seventh and one forty second. One half, one third, one eighth and one twenty fourth.
<bookmark mark='second'/>One half, one third, one ninth and one eighteenth. One half, one third, one tenth and one fifteenth.
<bookmark mark='third'/>One half, one fourth, one fifth and one twentieth. One half, one fourth, one sixth and one twelfth.
